chapter.name: Resources and Development
chapter.blurb: What makes something in nature a resource, and the several ways this book classifies resources; the idea of sustainable development traced from Gandhiji through the 1992 Rio Earth Summit; why resource planning must be balanced across India's unevenly endowed regions; how India's land is divided across relief features and land-use categories, and why net sown area and forest cover have shifted only modestly nationally since 1960-61 even though they vary hugely by state; the human and natural causes of land degradation and the measures used against it; the six major soil types the text and map describe; and the three kinds of soil erosion with the four conservation practices used to slow them.

scope_in.item: Define when something in the environment counts as a resource (technologically accessible, economically feasible, culturally acceptable) and state the chapter's four bases for classifying resources: origin (biotic/abiotic), exhaustibility (renewable/non-renewable), ownership (individual/community/national/international) and status of development (potential/developed stock/reserves)

Read Fig. 1.1 (the interdependent relationship linking human beings to nature/physical environment, technology and institutions) and Fig. 1.2 (the classification tree splitting resources into Natural -- Renewable [continuous/flow; biological, e.g. forests and wildlife] and Non-Renewable [recyclable, e.g. metals; non-recyclable, e.g. fossil fuels] -- and Human, classified by structures/institutions and by quantity/quality)

State the definition of sustainable development and describe the outcomes of the 1992 Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit (the Declaration on Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity, endorsement of the global Forest Principles, adoption of Agenda 21) and Agenda 21's own aim and its stated objective for local governments

Describe the chapter's history of resource-conservation thought: Gandhiji's words and philosophy, the Club of Rome (1968), Schumacher's book Small is Beautiful (1974), and the Brundtland Commission Report (1987, published as Our Common Future), which introduced the concept of Sustainable Development

Explain why planning matters for a resource-diverse country like India, using the chapter's regional examples (Jharkhand/Chhattisgarh/Madhya Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Ladakh), and explain why resource availability alone does not guarantee development without matching technology and institutional change, citing the colonisation example

State resource planning's three steps (identification/inventory via surveying and mapping; evolving a planning structure with technology, skill and institutions; matching plans with national development plans) and that India has pursued this since the First Five Year Plan
State India's land under relief features from Fig. 1.3 (plains about 43 per cent, mountains about 30 per cent, plateau about 27 per cent) and each relief type's stated significance

List the five land-utilisation categories (forests; land not available for cultivation; other uncultivated land excluding fallow; fallow lands; net sown area) with their sub-categories, and distinguish net sown area from gross cropped area

State India's total geographical area (3.28 million sq km) and why land-use data covers only 93 per cent of it; describe net sown area's national figure (about 54 per cent of the reporting area) and its state-to-state variation (over 80 per cent in Punjab and Haryana, under 10 per cent in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands); state that forest cover remains below the National Forest Policy (1952)'s 33 per cent target; and read Fig. 1.4's two pie charts for the nine listed land-use categories, the net sown area share (45.26 per cent in 1960-61 to 45.64 per cent in 2019-20) and the forest share (18.11 per cent to 23.41 per cent)

Explain how deforestation, overgrazing, mining/quarrying and over-irrigation cause land degradation, with the chapter's own state examples, and how mineral-processing dust and untreated industrial effluents add to land and water degradation

Describe the chapter's land-degradation conservation methods: afforestation and grazing management; shelter belts and sand-dune stabilisation in arid areas; and waste-land management, mining control and treated effluent disposal in industrial/suburban areas

Describe the soil profile's four layers from Fig. 1.5 (top soil, subsoil, substratum, unweathered parent bed rock) and the five factors of soil formation the chapter names (relief, parent rock, climate, vegetation and other life forms, time)

Describe each of the six soil types the chapter names (alluvial, black/regur, red and yellow, laterite, arid, forest) with their formation, location and use, and read the India: Major Soil Types map's own six-category legend (Forest and Mountainous, Alluvial, Red and Yellow, Black, Laterite, Arid)

Define soil erosion and describe its human causes (deforestation, overgrazing, construction, mining) and natural causes (wind, glacier, water), and its named forms (gully erosion/bad land/ravines in the Chambal basin; sheet erosion; wind erosion; erosion from up-and-down-slope ploughing)

Describe the chapter's four soil-conservation methods: contour ploughing, terrace cultivation (well developed in the western and central Himalayas), strip cropping, and shelter belts (which have helped stabilise sand dunes and the desert in western India)

concepts.name: Types and classification of resources
concepts.description: What makes something in the environment a resource, and the several bases -- the chapter's own four-part list and Fig. 1.2's classification tree -- on which resources can be sorted.
concepts.idea: Something in our environment becomes a 'resource' only when it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable to use; once it is, it can be classified on several different bases.
concepts.rule: The chapter gives four bases for classifying resources: (a) origin - biotic and abiotic; (b) exhaustibility - renewable and non-renewable; (c) ownership - individual, community, national and international; (d) status of development - potential, developed stock and reserves. Fig. 1.2 also gives a tree: resources are Natural or Human. Natural resources are Renewable (continuous/flow, e.g. wind and water; or biological, e.g. natural vegetation/forests and wildlife) or Non-Renewable (recyclable, e.g. metals; or non-recyclable, e.g. fossil fuels). Human resources are classified by structures and institutions, and by quantity and quality. Fig. 1.1 shows human beings at the centre of an interdependent relationship with nature (the physical environment), technology and institutions.
concepts.example: Wind and flowing water are Natural, Renewable, continuous/flow resources; metals are Natural, Non-Renewable, recyclable resources.

concepts.name: Development of resources and sustainable development
concepts.description: Resources were once treated as free gifts of nature and used indiscriminately; this concept traces how the idea of sustainable development emerged, from Gandhiji's own words through international efforts culminating in the 1992 Rio Earth Summit.
concepts.idea: Because resources were wrongly assumed to be free gifts of nature and used indiscriminately, causing depletion, inequality and ecological crises, sustainable development emerged as the corrective idea that development must not damage the environment or compromise future generations' needs.
concepts.rule: Sustainable economic development means development that does not damage the environment and does not compromise the needs of future generations. In June 1992, over 100 heads of state met at the Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit; they signed the Declaration on Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity, endorsed the global Forest Principles, and adopted Agenda 21 (also signed at the UN Conference on Environment and Development, UNCED) for achieving sustainable development in the 21st century; one major objective of Agenda 21 is that every local government should draw up its own local Agenda 21. Gandhiji said 'There is enough for everybody's need and not for anybody's greed', naming greedy individuals and exploitative technology as the root cause of resource depletion, and favoured production by the masses over mass production. The Club of Rome first systematically advocated resource conservation in 1968; Schumacher represented Gandhian philosophy again in his 1974 book Small is Beautiful; and the Brundtland Commission Report of 1987 made the seminal contribution of introducing the concept of Sustainable Development, later published as the book Our Common Future.
concepts.example: Indiscriminate use of resources, believed to be free gifts of nature, led to depletion, a rich-poor divide and global ecological crises such as global warming and ozone depletion -- exactly the problem sustainable development is meant to correct.

questions.q: The chapter names four separate efforts at resource-conservation thinking (Gandhiji, the Club of Rome, Schumacher, and the Brundtland Commission) before describing one formal international summit (Rio, 1992). questions.a: The sequence suggests the idea of sustainable development built up gradually over decades through individual thinkers and expert bodies restating and refining similar concerns, before it was formally adopted as government policy at an international summit. Advocacy by a thinker like Gandhiji or Schumacher shapes opinion and can influence later action but does not commit any government; a summit like Rio, where over 100 heads of state signed agreed declarations, creates a formal, binding commitment that countries are expected to act on, which is why the chapter treats 1992 as the culmination rather than the start of this history.
s: The gradual, decades-long build-up of the idea recognised

The whole point of Agenda 21 and the Brundtland Report's concept of Sustainable Development was to find a way to keep developing economically while protecting the environment and future generations' needs, not to force a choice between the two.

concepts.name: Resource planning in India
concepts.description: Because India's resources are unevenly spread across its regions, planning -- the widely accepted strategy for their judicious use -- has to balance resource-rich and resource-poor areas.
concepts.idea: India's resources are unevenly spread across its regions, so planning -- carried out as a three-step process -- has to balance resource-rich and resource-poor areas rather than treat the country as uniform.
concepts.rule: Resource planning is a complex process with three steps: (i) identification and inventory of resources across regions, through surveying, mapping and qualitative/quantitative estimation; (ii) evolving a planning structure with appropriate technology, skill and institutional set-up; (iii) matching resource development plans with overall national development plans. India has pursued these goals since the First Five Year Plan launched after Independence. The chapter illustrates regional imbalance with examples: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh are rich in minerals and coal; Arunachal Pradesh has abundant water but weak infrastructure; Rajasthan is well endowed with solar and wind energy but lacks water; the cold desert of Ladakh has rich cultural heritage but is deficient in water, infrastructure and some vital minerals, and is relatively isolated. This calls for balanced planning at national, state, regional and local levels. Resource availability alone is a necessary but not sufficient condition for development: without matching technology and institutional change, resource-rich regions can stay economically backward, while resource-poor regions can become economically developed -- as the history of colonisation shows, where colonisers' superior technology let them exploit colonies' resources and establish supremacy.
concepts.example: Rajasthan has plentiful solar and wind energy yet is short of water, which is why resource planning must be balanced across regions rather than applied uniformly.

concepts.name: Land resources and land utilisation
concepts.description: Land is a finite, non-substitutable resource that supports almost everything we do, so this concept breaks down how India's land is spread across relief features and put to different uses.
concepts.idea: Land is a finite resource used in several distinct ways, so the chapter breaks it down by relief feature and by a five-category land-utilisation scheme, and tracks how these shares have shifted over six decades.
concepts.rule: India's land lies under mountains, plateaus, plains and islands: about 43 per cent is plain (agriculture and industry), about 30 per cent is mountains (perennial river flow, tourism, ecological aspects), and about 27 per cent is plateau (rich reserves of minerals, fossil fuels and forests) -- shown in Fig. 1.3. Land is used for: (1) forests; (2) land not available for cultivation (barren/waste land; land under non-agricultural use such as buildings, roads, factories); (3) other uncultivated land excluding fallow (permanent pastures and grazing land; land under misc. tree-crop groves, not counted in net sown area; culturable waste land, left uncultivated over 5 agricultural years); (4) fallow lands (current fallow, uncultivated for a year or less; other than current fallow, uncultivated 1-5 years); (5) net sown area, the physical extent of land on which crops are sown/harvested -- area sown more than once in a year, plus net sown area, equals gross cropped area. India's total geographical area is 3.28 million sq km, but land-use data covers only 93 per cent of it, since most north-eastern states except Assam, and parts of Jammu and Kashmir occupied by Pakistan and China, are not fully surveyed. Counting in poor-quality/high-cost fallow-like land, net sown area comes to about 54 per cent of the reporting area nationally, but it varies hugely by state: over 80 per cent in Punjab and Haryana, under 10 per cent in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Forest cover remains far below the National Forest Policy (1952)'s desired 33 per cent of geographical area. Fig. 1.4's two pie charts compare nine land-use categories between 1960-61 and 2019-20; the clearest, largest slices are net sown area (45.26 per cent to 45.64 per cent, changing only marginally) and forest (18.11 per cent to 23.41 per cent).

concepts.name: Land degradation and conservation measures
concepts.description: Continuous use of land without proper conservation causes land degradation, but the specific human activity behind degradation differs from state to state, and the chapter names matching remedies.
concepts.idea: Continuous use of land without conservation causes degradation, and the chapter shows that the specific human activity responsible, and the matching remedy, differs from region to region rather than being one single problem.
concepts.rule: About 95 per cent of our basic needs for food, shelter and clothing come from land, which we share across generations. Human activities -- deforestation, overgrazing, mining and quarrying -- and natural forces both aggravate land degradation. Mining leaves deep scars and over-burden after sites are abandoned; in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha, mining-linked deforestation has caused severe degradation. In Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, overgrazing is a main reason for degradation. In Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, over-irrigation causes degradation through waterlogging, which raises soil salinity and alkalinity. Mineral processing (grinding limestone for cement, calcite/soapstone for ceramics) generates dust that retards water infiltration into soil; untreated industrial effluents are a major source of land and water pollution. Solutions: afforestation and proper grazing management; planting shelter belts, controlling overgrazing, and stabilising sand dunes with thorny bushes in arid areas; and proper management of waste lands, control of mining activity, and treated discharge/disposal of industrial effluents in industrial and suburban areas.
concepts.example: In Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, over-irrigation -- not mining or overgrazing -- is the chapter's named cause of land degradation, through waterlogging and rising salinity.

concepts.name: Classification of soil types
concepts.description: India's varied relief, landforms, climate and vegetation have produced several distinct soil types, each shaped by different formation factors and suited to different uses.
concepts.idea: India's varied relief, landforms, climate and vegetation have produced six distinct soil types, each formed by a different combination of factors and suited to different uses.
concepts.rule: Soils are classified by formation factors, colour, thickness, texture, age, and chemical/physical properties, into: Alluvial soils (most widespread, entire northern plains, deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra, extending into Rajasthan/Gujarat and the eastern coastal deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri; classified by age into old alluvial/Bangar and new alluvial/Khadar, Khadar being finer and more fertile; very fertile overall, rich in potash/phosphoric acid/lime, ideal for sugarcane, paddy, wheat and other cereals/pulses); Black soils (regur/black cotton soil, ideal for cotton, typical of the Deccan trap/basalt region of the northwest Deccan plateau formed by lava flows, covering Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and extending along the Godavari-Krishna valleys; extremely fine/clayey, moisture-retentive, rich in calcium carbonate/magnesium/potash/lime but poor in phosphoric content, develops deep cracks in hot weather, sticky when wet); Red and Yellow soils (develop on crystalline igneous rocks in low-rainfall eastern/southern Deccan plateau, also in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, southern middle Ganga plain and the Western Ghats' piedmont zone; red colour from iron diffusion, yellow when hydrated); Laterite soils (from the Latin 'later', meaning brick; develops under tropical/subtropical climate with alternating wet/dry seasons through intense leaching; deep, acidic (pH below 6.0), generally nutrient-poor; found in southern states, the Western Ghats region of Maharashtra, Odisha, parts of West Bengal and the north-east; humus-rich under forest, humus-poor under sparse vegetation; useful for tea and coffee after conservation, especially in the hilly areas of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu; red laterite in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala suits cashew); Arid soils (red to brown, sandy, saline; common salt obtained by evaporation in high-salt areas; lacks humus and moisture due to fast evaporation; lower horizons have Kankar restricting water infiltration; becomes cultivable after irrigation, as in western Rajasthan); concepts.name: Soil erosion and soil conservation
concepts.description: Soil forms and erodes at the same time, normally in balance; human activity and natural forces can tip that balance, and the chapter names specific practices that restore it.
concepts.idea: Soil formation and soil erosion normally proceed together in balance; when human activity or natural forces disturb that balance, the chapter's conservation practices work to slow the erosive force enough for the balance to hold again.
concepts.rule: Soil erosion is the denudation of the soil cover and its subsequent washing down. Soil formation and erosion normally proceed together in balance, but this balance is disturbed by human activities (deforestation, over-grazing, construction, mining) and by natural forces (wind, glacier, water). Running water cutting through clayey soils makes deep channels called gullies, turning the land into cultivation-unfit 'bad land' -- called ravines in the Chambal basin. Water flowing as a sheet over a large sloping area washes away the top soil, called sheet erosion. Wind blowing loose soil off flat or sloping land is wind erosion. Defective farming, such as ploughing up and down a slope, also causes erosion by forming channels for fast-flowing water. Conservation methods: ploughing along contour lines (contour ploughing) decelerates water flow down slopes; cutting steps into slopes to make terraces (terrace cultivation) restricts erosion, and is well developed in the western and central Himalayas; dividing large fields into strips, with strips of grass left between crops to break the wind's force, is strip cropping; and planting rows of trees for shelter (shelter belts) has significantly helped stabilise sand dunes and the desert in western India.

questions.q: The chapter says soil formation and erosion normally happen at the same time, in balance. Analyse how each of the four conservation methods named in the chapter (contour ploughing, terrace cultivation, strip cropping, shelter belts) works to restore that balance, rather than to stop erosion completely.
questions.a: Contour ploughing slows down, rather than eliminates, the speed of water running down a slope, reducing how much soil it can carry off. Terrace cultivation breaks a long slope into shorter, gentler steps, reducing the water's velocity and erosive power at each step rather than removing the slope. Strip cropping alternates crop strips with grass strips, so wind loses force gradually across the field instead of blowing unchecked. Shelter belts of trees similarly slow wind gradually over distance rather than blocking it entirely. In each case, the method manages the erosive force (water speed or wind speed) enough to let natural soil formation keep pace, restoring the normal balance between formation and erosion rather than trying to stop erosion outright, which would be impossible.
s: Contour ploughing's mechanism correctly explained as slowing water rather than stopping it
Terrace cultivation's mechanism correctly explained as reducing water's erosive power via shorter steps
Strip cropping and/or shelter belts' mechanism correctly explained as gradually reducing wind force
General conclusion drawn that these methods restore balance rather than eliminate erosion
